symptom: a vague ache low in the back
hook: the two kidneys had joined at the bottom into one big U
whatYouSee: Both kidneys sit low and their lower poles point inward and join across the spine into one U-shaped horseshoe.
whyItMatters: Horseshoe kidney is the commonest renal fusion anomaly. The lower poles fuse in the embryo and the isthmus gets caught under the inferior mesenteric artery so the kidney cannot ascend. It raises the risk of PUJ obstruction, stones, and infection.
treatment: Most people need no treatment. Complications such as obstruction or stones are treated when they occur.
takeaway: Low kidneys with medially pointing lower poles joined across the spine are a horseshoe kidney.

condition.symptom: a vague ache low in the back
condition.hook: the two kidneys had joined at the bottom into one big U
condition.keyFindings: Frontal intravenous urogram radiograph of the abdomen with contrast in both renal collecting systems, the bottom edge of the film above the pubic symphysis. Both kidneys lie lower and closer to the spine than normal with their long axes reversed so the lower poles point inward toward the midline. The lower poles join across the front of the lower lumbar spine through a band of kidney tissue (the isthmus), making one U-shaped kidney like a horseshoe. The calyces point medially and both ureters pass down over the front of the isthmus. The lumbar spine, psoas outlines and bowel gas look normal.

findings: Frontal (AP) abdominal radiograph with positive contrast opacifying both collecting systems, ureters and bladder, consistent with an excretory urogram/IVU-type or contrast study.
Kidneys appear fused across the midline: the lower poles are joined by a band of renal-density tissue (isthmus) crossing anterior to the spine at roughly L3-L4, producing a horseshoe configuration.
Lower poles are medially directed and joined; upper poles are separated and lie more laterally.
Renal pelves and calyces are opacified bilaterally with sharp calyceal contours; no obvious hydronephrosis or filling defect.

Both ureters are opacified along their full length, arising anteriorly/laterally from the pelves, running down near the lumbar spine and entering the bladder. They are mildly smooth in caliber with no definite obstruction.
Bladder is well opacified, smooth and rounded, with no clear filling defect.
Gas-filled colon and small bowel loops with stool are present. Gastric gas bubble is seen at the left upper abdomen. Hepatic shadow is on the right.

Osseous structures: lumbar spine and pelvis visible without an obvious acute fracture. The image is slightly rotated, with some overlying grid or line artifact over the right upper abdomen/chest wall.
differential: Horseshoe kidney with opacified collecting systems and ureters, without evident obstruction
Fused renal ectopia or other renal fusion anomaly (less likely)
Normal kidneys with a superimposed overlying soft tissue or bowel shadow simulating an isthmus (least likely)
anatomyConcerns: Midline renal fusion with low-lying kidneys is an anatomic variant (malrotation/fusion anomaly), not impossible anatomy.
Anterior ureteral course over the isthmus is expected in horseshoe kidney.
No impossible anatomy identified; slight rotation and grid/line artifacts are acquisition issues only.
